title: The Archival Arm
youtubeTitle: Selm Merel Wenselaers and the Quest for P1030680
description: Selm Merel Wenselaers, a historian, writer and curator based between Amsterdam and Antwerp, joined the P1030680 campaign and leads its archival arm. Much of that work is finding, connecting, and making operational material preserved by other researchers, collectors, and archivists. Michael Hörenberg's Breaking German Navy Ciphers project holds the message and the later allocation list. The Tafel A pairs are read from the Crypto Museum copy of the Quelle booklet (Prüfnr. 2499). She reconstructed the last days of U-534 and separated recovery from recipient. The surviving Quelle plan for 1 May (Tauschtafelplan Bruno, Prüfnr. 1772a) indicates Tafel A; edition compatibility with 2499 stays open: VROL NMKA → EACH/SEDM, drop the first E, ACH, K-Buch column 645. That still does not yield the machine setting, because the Grund table is missing. Rotor VIII on the fast wheel, across three same-day nets, would coincide about 1.6 percent of the time under a simple independent-choice model, and is read with the allocation lists as a question about how that day issued its keys. She independently rediscovered the crib filter that had dropped 99 percent of the corpus, chose the menus, and required a constellation so two linked stages were not glued into a sentence. Those questions ran and came back empty inside their printed scope: 28 of 28 twice, the BLEIBTBESETZT window, the NEUSTADT constellation, and the VIII-fast middle-ring arm (42 of 336 wheel orders; the other 294 stay open). The stripe the first cut of episode 4 left open was then consumed: 81 exact hits are split-menu ghosts, and 4,101 repairs (4,103 less two duplicate-shell skips) climbed to no break. A four-plug closer greets a known message in about 38 minutes only when the rotors are already right. Two further sweeps finished empty: the Thetis-register right-ring arm, 73 of 73, and the catalog from menu 418 under VIII-fast, 451 of 451. P1030680 remains unbroken. The next document is a 1 May key table, the Kenngruppenbuch (M.Dv.Nr. 98), a second Thetis signal, or the Grund table. Epoch C71.

scenes.headline: The archival arm
scenes.subhead: Selm Merel Wenselaers joined the quest.
scenes.voiceover: This episode is about a person who joined the campaign and changed it. Selm Merel Wenselaers is a historian, writer and curator, based between Amsterdam and Antwerp, and she leads the campaign's archival arm. The target is still P1030680: 72 letters, working assignment M-Thetis, 1 May 1945, still unbroken. What changed is the quest. She put the history of that day in hand: whose papers the sheet was found among, which table the indicators used, and how the keys of 1 May were assigned. Then the machine ran the questions she made worth running.

scenes.kicker: History · the boat and the sheet
scenes.headline: Found with the boat. Not proved for the boat.
scenes.subhead: Kiel, Helsingør, Copenhagen, Anholt. Recovery is not address.
scenes.voiceover: She reconstructed the last days of U-534: Kiel, then Helsingør and Copenhagen, then Anholt, from 1 May through 5 May 1945. The sheet we are attacking survives among that boat's papers, and she separated two facts that had been fused. Survival in the file is recovery, not proof the signal was addressed to U-534. A training-network signal the boat overheard, meant for someone else, is now an open hypothesis. A British interrogation report from April 1945, built on prisoner statements it says need confirming, describes boats in Baltic training having to come up and listen to scheduled broadcasts. That makes a radio-watch snapshot a plausible alternative to a folder of messages for U-534. The two are not ranked. It never names Thetis, and she does not let the training command, or a naval intercept station named Thetis, be equated with the key net M-Thetis. The recipient is now a question with a historian on it, not an assumption copied from an archive label.

scenes.headline: Neustadt and scuttling are one process.
scenes.subhead: Demolition parties stay. Crews transfer. Do not invent the sentence.
scenes.voiceover: She also changed what the plaintext is allowed to be. A crib is a guessed stretch of plaintext, and the campaign sweeps one only if it is attested in real traffic and at least 16 letters long. From named primary reports, fifteen boats were ordered toward Travemünde, with demolition parties left aboard and the rest of the crews sent to the training division at Neustadt. The war diary of U-3521, as she reports it, has the crew leaving for Neustadt on 2 May, except the demolition party. Those scans are not yet in hand, so that diary stays her report rather than a page the campaign holds. Her standard, now the campaign's, is that a named file is not a page in hand. The effect on the search is concrete. Neustadt and scuttling are one process, not two competing cribs. The machine may not glue them into a sentence nobody is attested to have sent, and it may not drop either string. Neustadt is eight letters, half the minimum. Her history is why it still had to be tested.

scenes.headline: VROL NMKA is not the word Thetis.
scenes.subhead: Key group, procedure group, book group. FORT is four letters.
scenes.voiceover: She brought in the navy's own indicator procedure, from the manual. A key group names which key a message uses. A procedure group, typed under the daily key, produces the message key. Both come from a book of groups, are enciphered again with a letter-pair table, and go on the air at the start of the message, repeated at the end. So the indicators point toward Thetis through a lookup in that book, not by spelling anything. VROL NMKA cannot be read as the plaintext word Thetis. The manual's rule for split messages inserts the marker FORT, but FORT is four letters, far too short to be a crib, and 72 letters is no evidence that this message is part of a longer one. The document she says to hunt is that book: the Kenngruppenbuch.

scenes.headline: 1 May is Quelle, Tafel A.
scenes.subhead: Day 1 is a printed A. The pairs are on a photograph.
scenes.voiceover: Tafel A is the documentary result. On a scan of the exchange-table plan Tauschtafelplan Bruno, kennwort Quelle, the column for May 1945 has day one as a clean printed A. That identifies Tafel A as the table indicated by the surviving Quelle plan for 1 May. She then put the pairs themselves on a photograph, from the Crypto Museum's copy of a Quelle letter-pair booklet. It turns V R into E S, O L into A E, N M into C D, and K A into H M. Stack the results and read across: the first letters spell EACH, the second SEDM. Drop the first letter of that first row and the key group is ACH, which the book places in column 645. ACH in column 645 still does not yield the machine setting, because the Grund table of starting positions is missing. What changed is provenance: a photograph, not a remembered mapping. One question stays open, and she defined it: the plan and the booklet share a kennwort but not a proof number, so they are not shown to be the same edition. None of this dates the M-Thetis assignment or yields a key. Across all 48 indicators in the campaign's corpus, which is one collection rather than the archives, ACH occurs only on this message, so there is no sister key to try.

scenes.headline: Rotor eight, on every fast wheel.
scenes.subhead: Three nets agree. Under a simple model, about 1.6 percent. The lists make it history.
scenes.voiceover: Rotor eight on the fast wheel is the historical result, and it belongs with the allocation lists. Every daily key recovered for 1 May puts rotor eight in the fast position, on three separate nets. Under a simple independent-choice model, that coincidence would occur about 1.6 percent of the time. Mechanically, rotor eight on the fast wheel leaves 42 of the 336 wheel orders, which is what made the middle-ring sweep affordable. It reorders the search. It does not close the other 294. Historically, it asks whether 1 May issued its fast wheel from one shared key table, and the allocation lists bear on the same question. An earlier allocation list, called Forelle, is reported to give book column 645 to Aegir. The later list shown by Michael Hörenberg's Breaking German Navy Ciphers project gives it to Thetis. Lists changed over time, so both can be true. The later list's date and provenance are still open, so M-Thetis stays a working assignment. Three nets is a thin sample, and these are only the keys that happened to be broken. The rotor agreement and those lists are the same problem: how this day issued its keys.

scenes.kicker: The journey · she made the inventory runnable
scenes.headline: 99 percent of the corpus never became a menu.
scenes.subhead: She independently rediscovered the filter, and chose the menus that can force a board.
scenes.voiceover: The tool that builds the catalog kept a phrase only when two or more decrypts carried it, which discarded 99 percent of the distinct phrases: 152,938 that appear only once. The catalog held what operators repeated, not the range of what they wrote. Those phrases expand to 2.6 million legal placements, too many to sweep blind. An internal audit had measured that gap in August, left a small test unrun, and never published it. On 22 September she independently rediscovered the same filter from outside, brought three historically motivated phrases, and reproduced the placements of the longest one exactly. Then she chose menus. A menu is the graph of constraints that one crib placement gives the Bombe, and its closed loops are what let it reject wrong settings. Of four placements tied for the most loops, she picked the two that stay in one connected piece. The other two split apart, which is the ghost shape from episode 4. She knew the phrases came from other nets, not Thetis. They were still the right experiment, because that dormant inventory had never had a historian on it.

scenes.headline: 28 of 28, and then 28 of 28 again
bullets: Exact board: 0 raw stops over 4.471×10¹¹ settings
Missing four-letter group: the same empty result
One mis-read letter: priced at ~20 h, not run, ranked below a document
scenes.voiceover: Those three phrases ran: a Lübeck strongpoint from the second net, a march to Neustadt that had already set off, and an order to set off for Neustadt immediately. That gave 28 placements, swept across every ring setting of the fast wheel, with the middle wheel's ring held at A. All 28 died at the board: zero stops, meaning not one of 447 billion settings survived. Rerun as if a four-letter group had gone missing, the kind of error found on a sister message, all 28 died again. Both readings of the transcript are closed for these placements. A single mis-read letter is still open. It was not run: on these menus it projects to zero stops, would cost about 20 hours, and ranks below a document. The negative is about these alignments in this ciphertext, and it proves her selection could be measured, which the unrun August test never was.

scenes.headline: Two anchors. Nothing asserted in the gap.
scenes.subhead: Bleibt besetzt is verbatim. Neustadt rides with it, not inside a fake line.
scenes.voiceover: The same-day radio phrase did not have to be reconstructed. She brought bleibt besetzt, remains occupied, with its FFFTTT prefix, and the repository already holds that string exactly, in message P1030668. The test used the exact 40-letter window around it: four alignments, each one connected piece. With rotor eight on the fast wheel and both the middle and fast rings swept, all four died at the board. That rules out those alignments in P1030680, inside 42 wheel orders. It does not touch the phrase in P1030668. Neustadt still could not be swept alone, and she would not invent a sentence joining it to the radio phrase. So the campaign learned a constellation: one menu that combines two separate anchors and asserts nothing about the gap between them. All 24 such menus died with zero stops. The history of the order stands. What failed is the claim that both strings sit verbatim in this ciphertext at those offsets. Those runs held the middle ring at A, which on wide spans leaves 12 to 23 percent of keys untested, and she ranked sweeping that remainder below a document.

scenes.kicker: The arm she and the machine both named
scenes.headline: The likeliest orders came back empty.
scenes.subhead: 24 catalog placements, 42 of 336 orders. No ring gap inside that prior. The rest stay open.
scenes.voiceover: The middle ring was the arm she and the mechanical side independently named next. Holding the middle wheel's ring at A misses any key whose middle wheel turns over inside the crib: roughly 8 to 15 percent of keys on a crib of 30 to 40 letters. The arm was graded first, and the blind control still breaks with both rings swept. Against this message, it ran the 24 strongest placements from the recurrence catalog, with rotor eight on the fast wheel. All 24 died, with zero stops. For those placements, inside those 42 orders, no ring gap remains. The other 294 orders stay open, so this is not wheel-order coverage. These are the historically likeliest orders, run because the rotor agreement and her lists made likelihood a question about a shared key table, and they came back empty.

scenes.headline: The stripe from episode 4, finished
bullets: 81 exact hits: split-menu ghosts, no consistent board
4,101 repairs climbed (two duplicates skipped), 3.33 million climbs, no break
Best −3.0390 is not a near miss against 12 noise samples
scenes.voiceover: This closes a loop from earlier in the series. The first cut of episode 4 stopped mid-stripe: one shell, meaning one fixed choice of wheels and rings, all 628 Futures, settings zero through 255, and thousands of candidates waiting to be replayed. That replay is done. All 81 exact hits are ghosts: their menus split into pieces that no single ten-plug board can satisfy. The 4,103 repaired candidates, less two duplicates, were climbed in three passes, the last alone running 3.33 million plugboard climbs. Every crib check failed. The best score beat a floor of 12 random settings, but after millions of climbs that is multiple comparisons, not a near miss. The lesson is procedural: a manifest should refuse disconnected Futures before a single setting runs.

scenes.kicker: A closer that waits on her setting
scenes.headline: 38 minutes, once the rotors are already right.
scenes.subhead: Known message greets. Wrong setting does not. This target was not entered.
scenes.voiceover: The software closer is real, but it can only finish what the history starts. Give it the true rotor setting of the known message P1030684, and it tries every four-plug board, climbs the rest, and in about 38 minutes one candidate clears the bar: the known plaintext, all 10 plugs. At a wrong setting, the same budget finds nothing. Letter frequency cannot shortcut those four plugs: in 32 controls, the commonest letters never held all four. Pointed at P1030680 without a known setting, the same brute force would take about 33 years per shell, so it was not launched. A true Bombe stop is finishable at this length. Finding the stop is the historical problem. Two other sweeps finished empty in the same stretch, and they are listed in the description.

scenes.headline: The quest is a document
bullets: A 1 May key table, or proof the fast wheel was assigned centrally
The Kenngruppenbuch, a second Thetis signal, or the Grund table
She sees the scope before the next GPU tranche
scenes.voiceover: Which brings the campaign to the quest she redefined. The compute had been going into whether a placement had been run. She moved the weight onto whether the hypothesis is the right historical object. The arithmetic says 72 letters are enough. The key is about 86 bits, the redundancy in 72 letters of German is about 230 bits, and unicity sits near 27 letters, so only the true key should read as German. If the transcript is sound, every negative so far is a failure of search, not of information. A second Thetis signal from the same day would put 144 letters against the same daily plugboard. She keeps the stories of this ciphertext separate: an ordinary M-Thetis message with a missing key, a signal overheard and meant for someone else, a repeat from an earlier day, an officer cipher inside an outer key, a stale key, or a message from a training circuit, a possibility she explicitly treats as unproven. The sheet fields that would choose among them never enter the Bombe: reception time, frequency, callsign, a repeat mark, and the neighboring sheets. So the documents that would move the search are a 1 May key table, the Kenngruppenbuch, a second Thetis message, and the Grund table. She has live enquiries out. A real reply outranks another GPU tranche, and before that tranche, the completed scope goes back to her. That gate is how the team works.

scenes.headline: The next move is a document.
scenes.subhead: P1030680 remains unbroken. She sees the scope before the next tranche.
scenes.voiceover: P1030680 remains unbroken. Selm Merel Wenselaers leads the archival arm, and much of what that arm holds was preserved by other people. Michael Hörenberg's Breaking German Navy Ciphers project holds this message and the later allocation list. The Tafel A pairs are read from the Crypto Museum's copy of the Quelle booklet. Researchers, collectors, and archivists are still helping, including where a lead is only provisional. What that work changed is which questions are worth a GPU run, and which ones need a document. The machine can finish a message once a setting is locked. It cannot invent the setting.
